# Memory Management

```{r}
#| include: false
## library to inspect objects
library(lobstr)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(rlang)
```

```{r}

a <- runif(1e6)
as.integer(obj_size(a))
as.integer(obj_size(list(a, a)))
```


(@) reassignment [does not create]{.warning} new objects.

```{r}
x <- c(1,2,3)
y <- x
obj_addr(x)
obj_addr(y)
ref(x)
ref(y)
```
- Can use either `obj_addr` or `ref`

(@) strict about syntactic names: only [characters]{.key}, [underscore]{.key}, [digits]{.key} and [dots]{.key} are allowed.
Can [only]{.warning} start with [characters]{.warning} or [dot but not followed by a number]{.warning}. 
In order to use [non-syntactic]{.warning} identifiers, use [backticks.]{.warning}
    
```{r}
`_abc` <- 1
`_abc`
`10` <- 15
`10`
```
(@) use `make.names` to convert to valid values. 
    
(@) use `check.names = F` option with `read.csv()` since we don't want R to convert column names internally using `make.names()`

(@) [copy-on-modify]{.key} objects are copied only when they are modified

    * Once duplicate object was created for y, it is the [single pointer]{.warning} to the new object. So, subsequent
changes [do not create]{.warning} any further objects. This is an example of [modify-in-place.]{.key}
```{r}
x <- c(1,2,3)
cat(tracemem(x), "\n")
y <- x # not here
y[[2]] <- 22
y[[3]] <- 24
untracemem(y)
```

(@) copy-on-modify triggered only when there are more than one name bound to an object. So, the following does not trigger any copies.

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, 3)
cat(tracemem(x), "\n")
x[[3]] <- 4
untracemem(x)
```
(@) function arguments follow copy-on-modify rule on the passed parameter too.
    
    * if the passed parameter is returned back without modification, this would be the same pointer that was passed.

(@) vector objects are created with values in place whereas [lists]{.warning} have [pointers]{.warning} to 
values created separately.

```{r}
vec <- c(1,2,3)
l <- list(1,2,3)

ref(vec)
ref(l)
```
(@) [copy-on-modify for lists]{.key} When lists are modified, they are [shallow copied]{.warning}.
This means that the copied list points to the old objects that were not changed. Only change is to the object that was.

```{r}
l1 <- list(1,2,3)
l2 <- l1
l2[[2]] <- 22
ref(l1, l2)
```
(@) [copy-on-modify for data frames]{.key} Dataframes has one pointer for each column 
    
    * [if column is modified,]{.key} copy-on-modify would mean a new dataframe will created with new references for each column. 
Unchanged columns will be shallow-copied i.e. reference to the unchanged column will be to the old memory of the column.
    * [if row modified,]{.key} Deep copy will occur. The new dataframe will have reference to two brand new memory addresses.

```{r}
df <- data.frame(a = 1:5, b = 11:15)
df1 <- df
df1[,2] <- df1[,2] * 2
ref(df, df1)
df2 <- df
df2[2,] <- df2[2,1] * 3
ref(df, df2)
```
(@) character vectors do not store values. They point to a [global pool of strings]{.warning}

```{r}
x <- c("a", "a", "abc", "ac")

ref(x, character = TRUE)
```

(@) [No use declaring an integer vector, since if any member is inadvertently allocated a double value,
it triggers a copy action whereby a double vector is created upcasting each value in the original 
]{.warning}
```{r}
x <- c(1L, 2L, 3L)
tracemem(x)
x[[3]] <- 4
untracemem(x)
```
(@) [Address extensions are not reported by `tracemem`]{.warning}. Note below that `x` was copied when 
we attempted to extend its size to 3. This is [true for both vectors and lists]{.warning}. The `tracemem` messages seen here
are due to qmd rendition. Track the memory id for accurate memory allocation.
```{r}
x <- list(1, 2)
obj_addr(x)
tracemem(x)
x[[3]] <- 3
obj_addr(x)
untracemem(x)

x <- c(1, 2)
obj_addr(x)
tracemem(x)
x[[3]] <- 3
obj_addr(x)
untracemem(x)
```

[Q. What happens when a list is allocated to itself as a member?]{.question}
shallow-copy of x pointing to the old copy of x. [Note: Ignore the extra copies internally created by
`ref` triggering the two extra `tracemem` messages.]

```{r}
x <- list(1,2)
ref(x)
tracemem(x)
x[[2]] <- x
ref(x)
```
(@) Repeated objects are counted only once

```{r}
x <- runif(1e6)
obj_size(x)
obj_size(list(x,x,x))
```
(@) [copy-in-place]{.key} when object is bound to only one name. Also, [environments]{.warning} are always modified in place.

[Q. What happens when `df[[1]] <- df[[1]] + 0.5` is called]{.question}
```{r}
df <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 11:20, z = 21:30)

cat(tracemem(df), "\n")
df[[1]] <- df[[1]] + 0.5
obj_addr(df)
untracemem(df)

```

R's [replacement function machinery]{.key} kicks in. The statement is replaced by 
[df <- `[[<-.data.frame`(df*, i, value)]{.warning}.

R creates 2 copies of the object:

- [original df ──copy──► temporary df*]{.warning} before entering the replacment function. This is special behaviour of the replacement machinery and not how it works for ordinary functions.
- [`[[<-.data.frame` is like an ordinary function whose argument x creates another reference beside the df* retained by the replacement machinery]{.warning}. So, when it is modified another 
copy is created.

[Q. If there are many columns are they need to be modified in a loop, what's the recommended pattern?]{.question}

Process the modification in a batch using `vapply` or `Map` and apply at a single shot using `df[]`. This will make the replacement machinery trigger only once.

```{r}
df <- data.frame(matrix(runif(5 * 10), ncol = 5))
medians <- vapply(df, median, numeric(1))

cat(tracemem(df), "\n")

df[] <- Map(\(x, m_i) x + m_i, df, medians)
# df[] <- vapply(df, \(x) x + 0.5, numeric(1))
untracemem(df)
```

[Q. Whats the difference between `df <- lapply(df, as.character)` and `df[] <- lapply(df, as.character)` ]{.question}

The first one allocates a new list to `df` whereas the later converts the columns to character as expected.
The benefit of `df[]` is that it retains the data frame structure. So, allocation of various length values such as a single scaler
or a vector of the same length as a row uses [recycling while respecting the data frame structure.]{.warning}

(@) Vector concatenation [flattens]{.warning} into a single vector.


```{r}
c(c(1,2,4), c(10, 11, 12))
```

(@) `typeof()` for getting the type of the vector. [Do not use]{.warning} `mode()` or `storage.mode()` as they are there for old code compatibility purposes.

```{r}
typeof(c(1L))
typeof(c(1))
typeof(c(TRUE))
typeof(c("Hello"))
```
(@) Only use the [lowest level type checkers]{.warning}. 

```{r}
is.integer(1L)
is.integer(1)
is.double(1)
is.logical(1)
is.logical(T)
is.character("1")
is.character(1)
```

(@) Every operation with `NA` leads to na [other than]{.warning} `NA^0`, `NA | TRUE` , `NA & FALSE`

(@) Test `NULL` and `NA` with `is.null()` and `is.na()`.

```{r}
is.null(names(1:10))
is.na(NA)
```
(@) Coercion rule: [Character > Double > Integer > Logical]{.key}.


```{r}
typeof(c(1L, TRUE))
typeof(c(1, 1L, TRUE))
typeof(c("1", 1, 1L, TRUE))
```

[Q. Use of `is.atomic()`, `is.numeric()` and `is.vector()`?]{.question}
- `is.atomic()`: Is it the object an atomic vector OR is it NULL?
- `is.numeric()`: Numeric vector (integer or double) AND NOT ANY(`factor`, `Date`, `difftime`, `POSIXt`)
- `is.vector()`: Vector AND no attributes other than names


(@) [Attributes]{.key}: Attributes are `Pairlist`. Get with `attr()` and `attributes()`. Set with `structure()`.
```{r}
x <- c(1,2,3)
is.vector(x)
x <- structure(
  x,
  a = "first",
  b = 2L
)
attributes(x)
is.vector(x)

```
(@) The `dim` attribute turns an atomic vector into a matrix. So, it is set using `structure()` the atomic vector can be converted to 
 matrix within using `matrix()` function.

```{r}
m <- structure(
  1:10,
  dim = c(5,2)
)

is.matrix(1:10)
is.matrix(m)
m
```
[Q. Common methods of atomic vectors, matrices, and array]{.question}
- *Vectors*: `c()`, `names()`, `length()`, `is.null(dim(x))`
- *Matrices*: `is.matrix()`, `colnames()`, `rownames()`, `nrow()`, `ncol()`, `rbind()`, `cbind()`, `t()`
- *Arrays*: `dimnames()`, `dim()`, `is.array()`

:::{.definition}
**S3 Atomic vectors** Vectors with `class` attribute. Ex. `factor`,`Date`, `POSIXct`, `difftime`. 
Some of these S3 vectors have other attributes as well.
:::




(@) `factor` are built over `integer` types, has `class` and `levels` attributes. [Non-existent
values]{.warning} can be part of the levels as well.

```{r}
x <- c("b", "a", "a", "a", "b")
table(x)
x_f <- factor(x, levels = c("a", "b", "c"))
table(x_f)
attributes(x_f)
```
(@) `Date`, `POSIXct` and `difftime` built over `double`. First two are no. of days and no. of seconds
since *1970-01-01* and the latter uses `unit` to store durations.
```{r}
today <- Sys.Date()
today
str(today)
dt <- as.Date("1970-02-01")
unclass(dt)

tm <- as.POSIXct("1970-01-02 12:00", tz = "UTC")
attributes(tm) <- NULL
tm

wk_1 <- as.difftime(20, units = "weeks")
str(wk_1)
```
- use `attributes(x) <- NULL` to get their undelying values.

[Q. How does `level` construction and array construction happen in factor?]{.question}

```{r}
f3 <- factor(letters, level = rev(letters))
f3
as.integer(f3)
```
 1. Numeric [level]{.warning} construction happens first. The numeric levels are from 1-26.
 2. The numeric levels are assigned to the [text labels]{.warning}. So, 1 is mapped to 'z', 2 to 'y' and so on. This is because 'letters' has been reversed.
 3. At this point the main vector is constructed. Since there exists a level, the first value 'a' is looked up against the labels of the level. It finds the corresponding
 level as '26' so it stores 26 and so on.

[Q. What happens when labels are reassigned using `levels()`]{.question}

```{r}
f <- factor(c("a", "b", "b", "c", "a", "b"))
f
levels(f) <- c("b", "c", "a")
f
```
 1. `levels` are constructed in the first `factor()` call along with labels. So, 1 $\rightarrow$ "a", 2 $\rightarrow$ "b"
 2. Main vector stores integer values (1,2,2,3,1,2)
 3. In the `levels(f)` call, levels are [re-leveled]{.warning}. So, 1 $\rightarrow$ "b", etc. 
 4. Finally, when `f` is printed, it prints the labels of the main vector based on the new labelling.

:::{.insight}
Factor levels often need to be rearranged so that the reference can be a particular category when dummy variables are defined during a regression exercise.
The statement `factor(x,levels=` does this correctly while the statement `levels(x) <-` means "rename the old labels into these new labels", which is wrong.
The **best** option is to make the intention clear by using `relevel(df$x, ref = "c")`
:::

```{r}
df <- data.frame(y = 1:10, x = c("a", "b", "a", "c", "a", "a", "b", "c", "c", "b"))

# CORRECT
# df$x <- factor(df$x, levels = c("c", "b", "a"))

# WRONG
# df$x <- factor(df$x)
# levels(df$x) <- c("c", "b", "a")

# BEST
df$x <- factor(df$x)
df$x <- relevel(df$x, ref = "c")
# str(df)
# df
model.matrix(~x, data = df)
```

[Q. How to convert a list to an atomic vector?]{.question} `unlist(lst)`. `unlist` strips **all** 
attributes and retains only the underlying value. The common type is the broadest type of all. 

```{r}
l <- list(a = 1:5, b = c("a", "b", "c"))
str(l)
typeof(l)
ref(l)
l <- unlist(l)
str(l)
typeof(l)
ref(l)
```

[Q. `typeof` on list returns?]{.question} `list`

[Q. Difference between `c(as.Date("1970-01-02"), as.POSIXct("1970-01-01 02:00", tz = "UTC"))` and `unlist(list(<a date>,<a posixct>))`?]{.question}

- `c`:
  1. considers what the type of the inputs are. In this case, they are `Date` and `POSIXct` respectively.
  2. Since, the first argument is Date, it retains the Date part of both i.e. converts the later to date.
  3. Retains the internal integer representation of date.

```{r}
d <- as.Date("1970-01-02")
dt <- as.POSIXct("1970-01-01 01:00", tz = "UTC")
unclass(c(d, dt))
# In this case d is converted to posixct and internally the double representation 
# stores the number of seconds.
unclass(c(dt, d))
```
- `unlist()`
  1. Strips all special information stored with the date/datetime objects.
  2. No date conversations as before. Just retains the [original]{.warning} double/integer values.

```{r}
unclass(unlist(list(d, dt)))
unclass(unlist(list(dt, d)))
```


(@) use `as_tibble()` to convert from `data.frame` to `tibble`

## Key features of `data.frame`

(1) [Both matrix-like and list-like]{.warning}: `rownames()` , `colnames()`, `nrow()`, `ncol()` work but so does `length()` which returns [no. of columns]{.warning}.
(2) `is.data.frame()` returns true for [both]{.warning} dataframe and tibble. But `is.tibble()` returns true [for only]{.{arning} tibbles.

## `tibble` > `data.frame`

(1) [No auto-conversion to factor]{.key} `stringsAsFactors = FALSE` [not needed]{.warning} to prevent string columns from being automatically converted to factors.

(2) [non-syntactic names]{.key} are not replace in tibbles.

(3) [recycling]{.key} only works with columns of size 1 in tibbles.

```{r}
# Data frame recycled if the largest one is 
# a multiple of all the other smaller ones. So, the below works fine.
df <- data.frame(x = 1:6, y = 1:2)
df

# This will throw an error
# tbl <- tibble(x = 1:10, y = 1:2)
```
(5) [columns during construction]{.key} Tibble allows reference to columns defined during construction.

```{r}
df <- tibble(
x = 1:3,
  y = x * 3
)
df
attributes(df)
```
(6) [auto conversion of single column selection]{.key} Single column selected `[` is [not converted automatically to vector]{.warning} in tibbles.

```{r}
df <- data.frame(
x = 1:3,
y = 11:13
)
# Autoconversion of single columns to vectors. This does not happen with tibbles.
df[,"y"]
df <- as_tibble(df)
df[,"y"] # Still a tibble
```
:::{.insight}
Use the list-style column access method `df[["y"]]` to directly get the **vector version** of a column. This makes intention clear. It works for **both `data.frame` and `tibble`**.
Equally, **always** use **drop = FALSE** with data.frame single columns access `df[,"y", drop = F]`
:::

```{r}
df <- tibble(
x = 1:3,
y = 11:13
)
df[["y"]]
```

(7) [simpler list-as-column]{.key} Including list as a column requires less code and is printed better

```{r}
df <- tibble(
x = 1:3,
y = list(1:2, 1:3, 1:4)
)
df
```
[Q. How do we include `list`, `matrix`, `array` in `data.frame`]{.question} 

Either [define separately]{.warning} or [use `I`]{.warning}. `I` means "leave it as-it-is."

```{r}
# This won't work
# df <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y = list(1:3, 1:4, 1:5))

# OPTION 1:
df <- data.frame(x = 1:3)
df$y = list(1:3, 1:4, 1:5)
df

# OPTION 2:
df <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y = I(list(1:3, 1:4, 1:5)))
```
(8) [Row names not supported]{.key} Tibbles do not support row names. We can use `rownames` attribute to convert to a column.


```{r}
df <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y = 21:23, row.names = c("first", "second", "third"))
tb <- as_tibble(df, rownames = "names")
tb
```

[Q. What happens when we transpose a dataframe?]{.question} data.frame is converted into a matrix.

[Q. Whats the difference between `as.matrix()` and `data.matrix()`]{.question}

`as.matrix()` uses the Char > Double > int > logical hierarchy. `data.matrix()` converts the values into [numeric values]{.warning}.

`data.matrix()` rules:

  1. *Characters*: convert into factors and return their internal values.
  2. *Factors*: Return internal integer values. 


```{r}
df <- data.frame(
  a = c("a", "b"),
  b = c(TRUE, FALSE),
  c = c(1L, 0L),
  d = c(1.5, 2),
  e = factor(c("f1", "f2"))
)

am <- as.matrix(df)
dm <- data.matrix(df)
am
typeof(am)
dm
typeof(dm)
```



# Subsetting

(@) When one of the elements in the boolean subset list is `NA`, the result is `NA`


```{r}
v <- c(10, 11, 12)
v[c(T, NA, F)]
```

## Subsetting Rules

||Matrix | List | Data frames
|---|---|---|---
`[]` with single selection criterion. eg. `item["x"]` or `item[var_x]`| [underlying vector sequence used]{.key} vector returned.| Returns list. Eg. lst["a"] | Behaves like list; returns data frames.
`[]` with double selection criterion. eg. `i[i[x] > 3, ]` or `item[,var_x]`| [Dimensionality reduction]{.key} Drops dimension if [either row or column is 1]{.warning}. Eg. both `m[1,]` and `m[,1]` would return vectors. Hence, [always use `drop = F`]{.warning}. || ▪ [No dim. reduction if row == 1]{.key}: `df[1,]` returns a data frame <br> ▪ [Dim reduction if col == 1]{.key}: `df[,1]` returns a vector. [Always use `df[1]`]{.warning} to select single column.
`[["a"]]` || [vector conversion]{.key}. [Recommended if vector conversion wanted]{.warning} | Behaves like list; [returns vector]{.warning}. 

```{r}
df <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = 11:15, z = 21:25)
col_df <- df[1]
v_df <- df[,1]
is.data.frame(col_df)
is.data.frame(v_df)
```
```{r}
df <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 11:20, z = 21:30)
s_df <- df[df$x == 1, ]
is.vector(s_df)
s_df
attributes(s_df)
```
:::{.insight}
1. **Matrices**: Always use `drop = F` when using double selection criteria. In these cases the dimensionality reduction is often unintended.
2. **Dataframe**: 
    - *Row selection*: No problem in using row selection criteria such as `df[df$x > 1, ]` as dimensions are not dropped for single rows. 
    - *Column selection*: mimic list; Use `df["c"]` to get column. If the vector is to be extracted, use `df[["c"]]`.
:::

[Q. What is the difference between `x[NA]` and `x[NA_real_]` ?]{.question} `NA` is boolean hence it is [recycled]{.warning} in the selection criteria. Therefore, 
a vector of `NA` are returned. On the other hand, `NA_real_` is real, so R only looks for the `NA_real_` th index and upon not finding it returns a [single]{.warning} `NA`.

```{r}
x <- 1:5
x[NA]
x[NA_real_]
```
(@) [Matrix in the selection criteria]{.key} 
    - Treats first and second columns as row and column index respectively. 
    - Returns a [vector]{.warning}.

[Q. Whats the difference between `df$x[] = list(NULL)` and `df$x = NULL`]{.question} The former sets all values of column `x` to `NULL` while the latter deletes `x`.
[Note the `list(NULL)`]{.warning}. This is needed as `NULL` by itself is a zero length vector.

```{r}
df <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = 11:15)
df$x[] = list(NULL)
df
df$x = NULL
df
```
[Q. How to get the diagonal of a matrix]{.question} Use the [matrix selection criterion]{.warning} property.

```{r}
df <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = 11:15)
diag_val <- min(nrow(df), ncol(df))
df

df[
  matrix(
  rep(seq_len(diag_val), each = diag_val),
    nrow = diag_val, byrow = T
  )
]
```

[Q. Consistent approach for subsetting of Non-existent indices?]{.question}
Use `pluck()` and `chuck()`. `pluck` returns `NULL` and `chuck()` throws an error.

[Q. lookup logic using `match()`]{.question} 


```{r}
grades <- c(1,2,2,3,1)

info <- data.frame(
grade = 3:1,
  desc = c("Excellent", "Good", "Poor"),
  fail = c(F, F, T)
)

info[match(grades, info$grade), ]
```

[Q. Random sample using `sample()`]{.question}


```{r}
set.seed(42)
df <- data.frame( x = c(1,2,3,1,2), y = 5:1, z = letters[1:5])
# reshuffled rows
df[sample(nrow(df)), ]
# Only 3 after reshuffling
df[sample(nrow(df), 3), ]
# 6 after replacement
df[sample(nrow(df), 6, replace = TRUE), ]

```
(@) `which()`, `intersect()`, `union()` are set functions whereas the boolean vectors, `&` and `|` are the corresponding 
boolean functions.

```{r}
x1 <- 1:10 %% 2 == 0
which(x1)

```
# Functions

[Q. How to call a function whose arguments are in a list?]{.question} `do.call`

```{r}
args <- list(1:10, na.rm = TRUE)
do.call(mean, args)
```
[Q. How to get the containing environment of a function?]{.question} `environment(myfunc)`

[Q. What are base R equivalents of purr functions `seek`, `map`, `map_int`, `map2 ` ]{.question}
`seek` = `Filter()`, `map` = `lapply`, `map_int` = `lapply() |> unlist()` and `map2` = `Map`. The base R functions have the 
function as the first argument. [Another important base R function is `sort(decreasing = TRUE)`.]{.warning}

```{r}
objs <- mget(ls("package:base", all = TRUE), inherits = TRUE)
funs <- Filter(is.function, objs)

n_args <- funs |>
  lapply(formals) |>
  lapply(length) |>
  unlist()

n_args |>
  sort(decreasing = T) |>
  head()

n_args <- funs |>
  Filter(f = \(x) !is.primitive(x)) |>
  lapply(formals) |>
  lapply(length) |>
  unlist()

sum(n_args == 0)
```
[Q. What does `length(NA)` and `length(NULL)` return?]{.question} 1 and 0 respectively.

(@) [Name resolution]{.warning} uses [lexical scoping.]{.key} This means that it uses parse-time rather than run-time dynamics using the concept of environments.
  1. Functions look for variables [in the environment they were defined]{.warning} not where they are called.

```{r}
f1 <- function() {
  x + y
}
f2 <- function() {
  x <- 10; y <- 11
  f1()
}
f2()
```
  2. [Dynamic lookup]{.warning} The latest value of a variable is used when looking up.

```{r}
x <- 10
f1 <- function() {
  x
}
f1()
x <- 15
# At this point value of x is changed. Now when the function looks up the value in its definition environment it fetches
# the variable with its latest values
f1()
```

(@) [Lazy evaluation]{.key} [of arguments]{.warning} 
  1. Uses the concept of [promise]{.key} data structure which is expression + environment against which it it evaluated + value (evaluated only one and stored)
  2. argument is evaluated only if/when it is accessed first in the function.
  3. [Different environment for default assigned arguments and those without]{.warning} Default uses the function execution environment 
  rather than the definition environment. This combined with lazy evaluation means the following works:

```{r}
f1 <- function(x = 1, y = x + 21, z = a + b) {
  a <- 22; b <- 23
  # z is lazily evaluated AFTER a and b are defined
  c(x,y,z)
}
f1()
```

```{r}
f1 <- function(x = ls()) {
  # the promise of x is constructed here. The environment it uses is the current exec env.
  # So it lists the objects in this environment not the global environment where f1() is executed.
  x
}
f2 <- function(x) x
f1()
f2(ls()) |> head()
```
[Q. Lazy evaluation - What does this print?]{.question}

```{r}
y <- 10
f1 <- function(x = {y <- 5; 2}, y = 0) {
  c(x, y)
}
f1()
y
```

(@) Closing connections with `on.exit(..., add = T)`, use the `after = FALSE` flag to execute the last defined first.

```{r}
f1 <- function() {
  on.exit(message("a"), add = TRUE, after = FALSE)
  on.exit(message("b"), add = TRUE, after = FALSE)
}
f1()
```

(@) Types of functions: [prefix, infix, replacement, special.]{.key}

(@) Priority of argument mapping [Exact match > partial match > position]{.key}

```{r}
f1 <- function(f, a, ba) {
  c(f = f, a = a, ba = ba)
}

# since f is taken out of the equation the next positional match is with the second argument
f1(2, 3, f = 1)
f1(b = 3, f = 1, 2)
```
# Environments

[Q. How to list all names bound by an environment?]{.question} `names()` for base R (`ls()` for old R) and `env_names(e1)` for new R.

[Q. What are the `rlang` functions for getting global, current, and empty environments?]{.question} `rlang::global_env()`, `current_env()`, `empty_env()`.
Use `identical(global_env(), current_env())` to check if the current environment is the global one.

[Q. How to get the full hierarchy of the current environment?]{.question} Use `env_parents()` with the `last` option set to the empty environment. 
Empty environment is [the only environment]{.warning} without a parent.

```{r}
e1 <- env(a = 1, b = "first")
rlang::env_parents(e1, last = empty_env())
```
[Q. `x<<-1` sets the value of `x` in the parent environment when it finds it. If it doesn't, where does it create x? ]{.question} In the global environment.
The `<<-` operator is most commonly used with function factories.

[Q. Consistent way to set and unset values using the rlang package]{.question} 
  - `env_bind(e1, a = 1)` which [binds in-place]{.warning}, hence no
assignment requirement. To unbind, `env_unbind(e1, "a")`. There are others ways too but inconsistent.
  - For base package, `e1[["a"]] <- 1` and `rm(e1, "a")`. To remove all from the current environment, `rm(names())`

```{r}
e1 <- env(a = 1)
env_bind(e1, b = 20)
# e1 was updated in-place without having to be assigned back to the environment variable
env_names(e1)
env_unbind(e1, "b")
env_has(e1, "b")
```
(@) Environment chaining begins with the [execution environment]{.key} for functions. Execution environment is the child of the [function environment]{.key}.
This extends all the way up to global environment.

```{r}
f <- function() {
  function() {
    print(current_env())
    print(env_parents(current_env()) )
  }
}
f()()
```
[Q. What's the difference between a function binding an environment vs the environment it is bound to?]{.question} 

  - Every function [binds an environment]{.warning}. This is a called the [function environment]{.warning}.
  - The function environment is the environment the function was [defined in]{.warning}.
  - This can be different from the environment the function is [bound to]{.warning}. For eg.

```{r}
func1 <- function() {
}
e1 <- env()
env_bind(e1, f = func1)
# function bound to the name f in the environment e1
env_names(e1)
# function environment: global environment. This the environment func1 binds
fn_env(func1) # or environment(e1)

```
  - Use `fn_env(func)` or `environment(func)` to get the function environment.
  - Function environment is the parent of the execution environment. 

[Q. Whats function environment(environment that the function binds) of `func`? whats the environment it is bound to?]{.question}

```{r}
x <- 50
f <- function() x + 1
f2 <- function() {
  x <- 20
  func <- f
  func
}
f2()()
```
The function environment is Global Env while the function it is bound to is the execution environment of f2.

(@) Every [package]{.warning} defines a [Package environment]{.key} and a [Namespace environment]{.key}. 

  - Package env. is [how callers find functions in the package]{.key}, all functions defined in it, forms part of the [search path]{.key} when a function is imported,
  and parent env is the package imported just before. 

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR

GlobalEnv --> N["Import n (Package env)"] 
N --> N1["Import n-1 (P env)"]
N1 --> Base["Base (P env)"]
Base --> EmptyEnv

```
  - Namespace environment is how package functions themselves find dependencies. Search starts with the package's own NS env file.
  The [imports]{.key} env is based on **imports** file.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR

NS["Namespace env"] --> I["imports env"]
I --> Base["Base (NS env)"]
Base --> GlobalEnv

```
  - [stacks]{.key} and [frames]{.key} are the execution data structures. Each frame points to the [execution env of the corresponding function.]{.warning}


(@) Use `invisible` to return value that is not printed by default.
```{r}
f1 <- function() {
  x <- 21
  invisible(x)
}
f1()
a <- f1()
a
```

## Environment functions

||`rlang` | Base R | 
|---|---|---|
creating an env | `env(parent = e1, a = 1)` | `new.env()`
getting bindings of env | `env_names(e1)` | `names(e1)` or `ls()`
current env | `current_env()` | `environment()`
global env | `global_env()` | `globalenv()`
empty env | `empty_env()` | `emptyenv()`
function env | `fn_env(func1)` | `environment(func1)`
getting parent of an env | `env_parent()` | `parent.env(e)`
getting [all parents until empty]{.warning} | `env_parents(e1, last = empty_env())` |
checking if a binding is present | `env_has(e1, "a")` |
binding an env | In place: `env_bind(e1, a = 1)` | In place: `e1[["a"]] <- 1`
unbinding | `env_unbind(e1, "a")` | 


# Conditionals

:::{.insight}
Difference between `cat("Hi\n")` and `message("Hi")` is in the intended purpose.
`cat` when the primary purpose of the function is to print whereas `message` when the developer chooses to print.
:::

(@) With `tryCatch` execution stops at the point the handled condition is encountered, where as with `withCallingHandlers`,
the execution returns to the point the condition was encountered.


```{r}
tryCatch(
  message = function(cnd) cat("Message encountered\n"),
  {
    message("First message")
    message("Second message")
  }
)

withCallingHandlers(
  message = function(cnd) cat("CH: message encountered\n"),
  {
    message("First message")
    message("Second message")
  }
)
```

(@) Warnings are usually collated and [printed right at the end.]{.warning}

```{r}
withCallingHandlers(
  warning = function(cnd) cat("Caught a message\n"),
  {
    warning("First message")
    warning("Second message")
  }
)
```

[Q. How to convert warning to an error?]{.question}

```{r}
warn2error <- function(expr) {
  tryCatch(
    warning = function(cnd) abort(paste0("****", conditionMessage(cnd), "****")),
    expr
  )
}
try(
  warn2error(
    {
      x <- 2^4
      warn("Hello")
    }
  )
)
```
# Functionals

(@) Use [functionals]{.key} like `lapply()` to apply a function to a group of elements rather than using for loops.
Functionals are functions that take a function as an input and return a vector.

(@) Use `vapply(lst, mean, na.rm = T, FUN.VALUE = numeric(1))` instead of `sapply()` to convert a list output to double like
`purrr:map_dbl`. 

[Q. How to get each element satisfying a certain criteria from a list of lists?]{.question} Use `map`. Also, use
the `.default` option to get a default value if the selection criteria does not satisfy.

```{r}
l = list(
  list(x = 1, y = c(2,1), z = 10),
  list(x = 2, y = c(3,1), z = 10),
  list(x = 3, y = c(4,1,2), z = 12),
  list(x = 21)
)
# Get value of all elements named "x" in a vector
l |> map_dbl("x")

# Get first element of all elements named "y". 
l |> map_dbl(list("y", 1), .default = NA)
```

(@) Use the base `split` function to split dataframes based on values of a column. 
Remember that [`paste0` is a vector function]{.warning}. It works individually to elements of a vector.

```{r}
tdir <- "testdir"

if (dir.exists(tdir)) fs::dir_delete(tdir)

dir.create(tdir)

#file.path with add the operating system based path separator automatically
cyls <- split(mtcars, mtcars$cyl)
filepaths <- file.path(tdir, paste0("cyl-", names(cyls), ".csv"))
walk2(cyls, filepaths, write.csv)

dir(tdir)
```
[Q. How to pass different values for an argument that is not the first one, for. eg. different `trim` values for `mean`?]{.question}
Use `pmap()`; define named list with name as `trim` in this case.

```{r}
trims <- list(trim = c(0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4))
pmap_dbl(trims, mean, x = runif(1000), na.rm = TRUE)
```
[Q. How to run a model on a list of datasets and get the adjusted R-squared?]{.question}

```{r}
cyls <- split(mtcars, mtcars$cyl)
cyls |> 
  map(\(x) lm(mpg ~ wt, data = x) |> summary()) |>
  map_dbl("adj.r.squared")
```

## Map Variants

||List | Atomic | Same type | Nothing|
|---|---|---|---|---|
One argument | `map()` | `map_dbl()`... | `modify()` | `walk()`
Two arguments | `map2()` | `map2_dbl()` ... | `modify2()` | `walk2()`
one arg + index | `imap()` | `imap_dbl()` ... | `imodify()` | `iwalk()`
N args | `pmap()` | `pmap_dbl()` ... | `pmodify()` | `pwalk()`


[Q. Get the sd of all numeric columns of palmerpenguins::penguins. Also, get the number of levels of each factor column.]{.question}

```{r}
pgs <- palmerpenguins::penguins

# sd of numeric columns
isnumer <- pgs |> map_lgl(is.numeric)
pgs[isnumer] |>
  map_dbl(sd, na.rm = T)

# length of factors
isfac <- pgs |> map_lgl(is.factor)
pgs[isfac] |>
  map_dbl(\(x) levels(x) |> length())
```

[Q. Create bootstrap samples of `mtcars`, fit the model `mpg ~ disp` to each and get the adjusted R squared for each]{.question}


```{r}
bootstrap <- map(1:10, \(x) mtcars[sample(nrow(mtcars), replace = TRUE),])
bootstrap |>
  map(
    \(x) lm(mpg ~ disp, data = x) |> summary()
  ) |>
  map_dbl("r.squared")
```


[Q. Why does `modify()` recycle the same value `nrow(mtcars)` times?]{.question}
Because it is programmed to return the same structure, including the number of rows and columns. 
```{r}
mtcars |> modify(1) |> head(5)
# Only one row in the data frame when using map
mtcars |> map(1) |> as.data.frame()
```

(@) Use `reduce()` to repeatedly apply a function to the result and next value of the list. 
```{r}
map(1:4, ~ sample(1:10, 15, replace = T)) |>
 reduce(intersect)

```
